title: Elephants know themselves in a mirror
hook: An Asian elephant named Happy looked in a mirror and touched a mark on her head.
peek: In 2006, researchers put a giant mirror in an elephant enclosure at the Bronx Zoo. One elephant, Happy, kept touching a painted mark she could only see in her reflection, a classic sign of self-recognition.
lede: In 2006, Joshua Plotnik, Frans de Waal and Diana Reiss set up a mirror about 2.5 metres tall in the elephant yard at the Bronx Zoo in New York. Three Asian elephants inspected it, checked behind it and watched themselves move. Next, the researchers painted a large white X on each elephant's head, visible only in the mirror. One elephant, Happy, kept touching it with her trunk.

bullets.text: The test was devised by the psychologist Gordon Gallup in 1970 with chimpanzees. An animal that uses a mirror to investigate a mark on its own body seems to understand that the reflection is itself.

Earlier studies had found no sign of self-recognition in elephants, but they used small mirrors placed out of reach. Plotnik's team built a big, sturdy one the elephants could walk up to, touch and look behind.

Happy paid far less attention to a matching control mark made with clear paint, so it was the sight of the X that drew her, not its feel. The other two elephants, Maxine and Patty, did not touch their marks.
Missing the mark does not show an animal lacks self-awareness. It may simply not care about a spot of paint, or may not have noticed it, which is why one clear pass counts for so much.
